intro/hello: This lecture is about the vision transformer, V I T for short, from Google, in twenty twenty.
intro/convs: In the ConvNets chapter, every design choice encoded a belief about images.
intro/beliefs: A filter looks only at a small neighborhood, and the same filter slides over every position.
intro/tf: The transformer, meanwhile, took over language with one generic operation, self-attention, that assumes almost nothing.
intro/question: So the V I T paper asked a blunt question. What if we feed an image to a standard transformer, and change as little as possible?
intro/answer: The answer is in its title: an image is worth sixteen by sixteen words. Cut the image into squares, and treat each square as a word.
intro/result: With enough training data, this matched or beat the best ConvNets of the time.
intro/plan: We will build it piece by piece, look inside a tiny trained one, and ask what it gave up by dropping those beliefs.
patches/seq: A transformer reads a sequence. The most literal way to make an image a sequence is to make every pixel a token.
patches/count: A two hundred and twenty four by two hundred and twenty four photo has about fifty thousand pixels.
patches/square: But attention compares every pair of tokens, so its work grows with the square of the length: two and a half billion pairs per layer.
patches/group: So V I T groups the pixels first. Cut the image into a grid of squares, P pixels on a side. These are the patches.
patches/cifar: Here is a real see-far ten image, thirty two pixels square. With eight pixel patches, it becomes a four by four grid.
patches/order: Read the patches left to right, top to bottom, like words on a page. That is the sequence.
patches/unroll: Then unroll each patch into one long row of numbers: every pixel, three colors each.
patches/vit: A full size photo with sixteen pixel patches makes a hundred and ninety six patches, each seven hundred and sixty eight numbers long.
patches/cheap: That is a long paragraph, not a book. Attention gets sixty five thousand times cheaper than with pixels.
patches/dial: The patch size is a dial. Halve it: four times the patches, sixteen times the attention work, but finer detail in every token.
patches/names: Model names record the choice. V I T, B sixteen is the base model, on sixteen pixel patches.
tokens/width: A patch is now a row of seven hundred and sixty eight numbers. But the transformer wants rows of its own width, which we call D.
tokens/E: One learned matrix, E, maps every patch to a vector of length D. That vector is the patch's token.
tokens/filters: Each column of E has one weight per number in a patch, so it folds back into a little color picture: a filter.
tokens/conv: In fact, multiplying every patch by E is a convolution, with a filter the size of a patch, jumping a whole patch at a time.
tokens/little: That single convolution at the bottom, with no overlap, is almost all V I T keeps from ConvNets.
tokens/cls: Next, a class token goes in front, borrowed from bert. It has no pixels of its own, and its final state will hold the answer.
tokens/pos: Last, every slot gets a learned position vector, added to its token, because attention by itself has no idea where a patch came from.
tokens/learned: The class token and the position vectors start as random numbers, and backpropagation trains them like any other weight.
tokens/z0: The result, z zero, has one row for the class token and one for each patch. That is the sequence the encoder reads.
encoder/same: From here on, V I T is the transformer encoder, unchanged.
encoder/recap: Recall self-attention. Every token makes a query, a key and a value.
encoder/recap2: Each token's output is an average of all the values, weighted by how well its query matches each key.
encoder/block: A block wraps attention and a small M L P in residual connections, with a layer norm in front of each.
encoder/only: Attention is the only place where patches see each other. And from the first layer, any patch can read from any other, however far apart.
encoder/mlp: Everything else treats each token on its own, the same way in every slot.
encoder/stack: Stack the block L times. The base model has twelve layers, each seven hundred and sixty eight wide: about eighty six million parameters.
encoder/head: At the top, the class token's final vector goes through a linear classifier, trained with the usual softmax loss.
encoder/reads: The class token starts as the same vector for every image. Layer by layer, it reads what it needs from the patches.
encoder/tiny: To look inside, we will use a tiny V I T: four pixel patches, six layers, trained on see-far ten, and right eighty one percent of the time.
cls/table: Each layer's attention weights form a table. Row i says how much token i takes from every token, and each row adds up to one.
cls/row0: Row zero belongs to the class token. Lay its sixty four patch weights back on the grid, and you see where it looked.
cls/image: Here is a test image the model never saw. Bright patches got more of the class token's attention, and dark ones got less.
cls/layers: Every layer and every head makes its own map. Early on, the class token has nothing to read but the raw patches.
cls/deeper: Deeper layers read from patches that have already mixed with their neighbors, so a single map is hard to interpret.
cls/chain: Attention rollout chains the layers: it multiplies their tables, counting the residual path as half of every step.
cls/object: It estimates how much of the final class token traces back to each input patch. Often, it lands on the object.
cls/others: Here are a few more test images, each with the model's guess.
cls/caution: Treat these maps as evidence, not explanation. They show where information was read from, not what the network did with it.
set/strange: Here is a strange property of the encoder. Nothing in it looks at which slot a token sits in.
set/why: Attention weights come from dot products between tokens, and everything else treats every token alike.
set/shuffle: Shuffle the patch tokens, and the outputs shuffle the same way, otherwise unchanged. The class token comes out exactly the same.
set/bag: Without positions, the encoder sees a set, not a sequence: a bag of patches.
set/two: To see this, two tiny models were trained the same way: one with position embeddings, and one without.
set/scramble: Shuffle the patches. The model with positions sees a scrambled picture, and changes its mind.
set/same: The model without positions gives exactly the same answer, for every one of the sixty four factorial orderings.
set/still: And it still gets seventy three percent of test images right, from colors and textures alone.
set/break: Position embeddings break the symmetry. The same patch in two slots becomes two different tokens.
positions/random: The position embeddings are one learned vector per slot. They start random, and nobody says the slots form a grid.
positions/compare: So compare them: for each slot, how similar is its vector to every other slot's?
positions/grid: Draw one slot's similarities as a little map, and put all the little maps on the grid.
positions/init: At initialization there is nothing to see. Each vector resembles only itself.
positions/trained: After training, neighboring slots have similar vectors, and each slot resembles its own row and column.
positions/found: The model found the two dimensional layout of the image from data alone.
positions/paper: The V I T paper saw the same thing, and found that building two dimensional positions in did no better than plain learned ones.
positions/resize: One catch: they exist only for the training grid, so to fine-tune on bigger images, V I T interpolates them onto a bigger grid.
bias/define: Every learning algorithm prefers some solutions before it sees any data. That preference is called its inductive bias.
bias/local: A ConvNet's bias is strong, and made for images. Locality: a small filter sees only a small neighborhood.
bias/share: Weight sharing: one filter is reused everywhere, so a feature learned in one corner works in every corner.
bias/equi: And as a consequence, translation equivariance. Slide the image, and the feature maps slide along with it.
bias/exact: Filter then shift, or shift then filter: the same answer, for every shift.
bias/vit: V I T keeps almost none of this. Slide the image by one pixel, and every patch now holds a different mix of pixels.
bias/four: Slide it by a whole patch, and the patches come back, but in new slots, with new position vectors added.
bias/global: And attention is global from the first layer. Nothing says that nearby patches should matter more.
bias/learn: So locality, nearness and the meaning of a shift all have to be learned, from data.
distance/measure: Did the model learn to look locally? The V I T paper measured each head's mean attention distance.
distance/how: For each patch, weight every patch it attends to by its distance in pixels, and average.
distance/rf: It plays the role of a receptive field. A head that looks only at its own patch scores zero.
distance/chart: Here is every head of the tiny model, layer by layer. The dashed line is what evenly spread attention would give.
distance/ours: In the tiny model, layer two is the most local, and from there the distance grows with depth. But every head stays near the even spread.
distance/paper: The paper found the same pattern in its large models: low layers mixing local and global heads, and distance growing with depth.
distance/learned: In the large model, many early heads learned to look locally, like a ConvNet's first filters. Nobody built that in.
distance/hybrid: Those local heads were rarer when a ResNet ran first, as if they did the job of early convolutions.
data/head: A strong inductive bias is a head start. If the assumptions are right, the model does not have to learn them, so it needs less data.
data/ceiling: If they are slightly wrong, they become a ceiling. A weak bias is the reverse: it needs more data, and it can gain more from it.
data/exp: The V I T paper made this trade visible, pretraining transformers and ResNets on three ever larger datasets, then testing on ImageNet.
data/in1k: With ImageNet alone, about a million images, the ResNets won. The large V I T even did worse than the small one.
data/in21k: With ImageNet twenty one K, fourteen million images, they were roughly level.
data/jft: With J F T three hundred M, Google's internal set of three hundred million images, V I T pulled ahead.
data/top: At the top, the huge V I T reached about eighty eight and a half percent on ImageNet, level with the best ConvNets, for less compute.
data/lesson: Convolution's bias helps when data is scarce. With enough data, learning the patterns directly is enough, and even better.
deit/problem: That left a practical problem. Few people have three hundred million labeled images.
deit/deit: Two months later, D E I T, from Facebook AI, trained a V I T on ImageNet alone, on one machine with eight G P Us, in under three days.
deit/recipe: The architecture was the same. What changed was the recipe.
deit/aug: First, heavy augmentation: random crops, color changes, and blending images and labels together, with mix up and cut mix.
deit/biasdata: Augmentation is inductive bias, delivered through data. A flipped copy with the same label says: flips do not change the class.
deit/reg: Second, strong regularization, and long training.
deit/token: Third, distillation. A second learned token sits beside the class token, and its job is to agree with a teacher network.
deit/loss: The loss is half the usual cross entropy with the true label, and half cross entropy with the teacher's top guess.
deit/teacher: The best teachers were ConvNets. The student, it seems, inherits some of the teacher's inductive bias.
deit/result: The result competed with ConvNets of similar speed, trained on the same data.
swin/other: The other route is to put some image structure back into the architecture.
swin/hybrid: The V I T paper itself tried a hybrid: a ResNet first, then the transformer on its feature map.
swin/swin: The most influential design is the swin transformer, from Microsoft Research Asia, in twenty twenty one.
swin/windows: First, windows. Attention runs only inside small windows of seven by seven patches, so a token sees only its neighborhood.
swin/cost: Locality is back, and the cost grows with the number of patches, not with its square.
swin/shift: To let information cross window borders, every second block shifts the windows by half a window.
swin/merge: Second, a hierarchy. Between stages, each two by two group of tokens merges into one, so each window covers four times as much.
swin/pyramid: That builds a pyramid of feature maps, like a ConvNet's, so swin slots straight into detectors and segmenters.
swin/convnext: The traffic went both ways. In twenty twenty two, ConvNeXt modernized a ResNet with ideas borrowed from transformers, and matched swin.
swin/lesson: Much of the gap, it turned out, came from training recipes and design details, not from attention itself.
outro/recap: To sum up: V I T cuts an image into patches, projects each one, adds a class token and learned positions, and runs a standard encoder.
outro/set: Without positions, the encoder sees a set, and all knowledge of the layout has to be learned.
outro/bias: V I T trades inductive bias for flexibility. It has to learn locality, and it does, but that costs data.
outro/close: With enough data, it wins. With less, a better recipe closes the gap, as in D E I T, or windows put locality back, as in swin.
outro/today: Today the plain V I T is everywhere: inside clip, masked autoencoders, and diffusion models.
outro/end: The lesson reaches beyond images. The less a model assumes, the more it has to learn from data, and the more it can learn.
